articles.title: Your tipster's record is a screenshot. I built one that can't be edited.
articles.excerpt: Everyone who posts football picks has a great record. That is not because they are all good at it. It is because the record is a screenshot, and screenshots are taken after the fact. The move is alway…
articles.body: Everyone who posts football picks has a great record. That is not because they are all good at it. It is because the record is a screenshot, and screenshots are taken after the fact. The move is always the same. Post the wins, delete the losses, quietly nudge the confidence number up in the image. Nobody can prove the pick did not say 0.78 at the time. The format has no memory of its own, so the tipster is the memory. I wanted to see what happens when the record lives somewhere the tipster does not control. This post is about the build: an agent that seals its picks to Walrus Memory before kickoff, seals the grade after full time, and cannot move the hash in between. It is called Receipts.
articles.author: Harish Kotra (he/him)

articles.title: AI Agent Guardrails Example: Copy-Paste Claude Code Rules
articles.excerpt: Originally published at Unattended. Here is a working AI agent guardrails example for Claude Code. Use deny rules in .claude/settings.json to block dangerous tools, a PreToolUse hook that exits with c…
articles.body: Originally published at Unattended . Here is a working AI agent guardrails example for Claude Code. Use deny rules in .claude/settings.json to block dangerous tools, a PreToolUse hook that exits with code 2 to catch the destructive commands those rules miss, and the --max-turns and --max-budget-usd flags to cap loops and spending. Each layer covers a different failure. Together they let a scheduled run work without someone watching it. Claude Code's hooks give you, in Anthropic's words, " deterministic control: certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them ." So a guardrail written as a hook doesn't depend on the model remembering an instruction. Which option is right for you? The right first guardrail depends on how you run Claude Code today.

articles.title: Linux MPTCP Inventory: Turning a 3.1 Million Product Match into a Review Queue
articles.excerpt: Linux MPTCP Inventory: Turning a 3.1 Million Product Match into a Review Queue A broad search result can create more work than clarity. ZoomEye returned 3,138,477 matches for product="Linux" while res…
articles.body: Linux MPTCP Inventory: Turning a 3.1 Million Product Match into a Review Queue A broad search result can create more work than clarity. ZoomEye returned 3,138,477 matches for product="Linux" while researching CVE-2026-98438, and the exact CVE filter returned 0. The product count is a useful map of Linux fingerprints. It is not a list of vulnerable MPTCP endpoints, and the review process needs to make that distinction explicit. CVE-2026-98438 is an uninitialized checksum bug in mptcp_write_data_fin() . The issue was introduced in Linux 7.1 and fixed in 7.2.7 and 7.3-rc3. A zero-length DATA_FIN with checksum negotiation can cause the kernel to calculate a packet checksum before ext->csum has been set.
articles.author: johnettagaweraks

articles.title: How VFlash Turns Robots into Sprinters in Just 1 ms
articles.excerpt: VFlash — Fast, Accurate Visual Planning Powered by Flash Primitive Decoding “A 1 ms planning step turns a robot from a slow‑poke to a sprinter.” – Lina Wu, MIT CSAIL Robots now stall because their bra…
articles.body: VFlash — Fast, Accurate Visual Planning Powered by Flash Primitive Decoding “A 1 ms planning step turns a robot from a slow‑poke to a sprinter.” – Lina Wu, MIT CSAIL Lead Robots now stall because their brains can’t think fast enough. Traditional visual‑language models (VLMs) decode plans token by token, dragging the control loop to 10 ms + per inference even on a top‑tier GPU. VFlash collapses the whole plan into a handful of geometric primitives and delivers a full motion plan in roughly 1 ms , while nudging accuracy up 3–5 percentage points on benchmark suites. The result is a real‑time visual planner that turns a natural‑language command into executable robot motion with no post‑processing lag.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 8, 2005: Europe launches Venus Express, its first mission to Venus
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. Here's why Venus Express mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express. Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years. During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole . It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes . Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras . These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere. Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this.

articles.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
articles.excerpt: By modeling how a planet without life develops its atmosphere, astronomers hope to be able to better distinguish rocky planets without life from those that are inhabited.
articles.body: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.
